newsitem.title: USA: Three-fourths of major U.S. cites restrict begging.
newsitem.headline: Three-fourths of major U.S. cites restrict begging.

text.p: In some U.S. cities it is illegal to lie down on a public sidewalk and others have designed park benches so they cannot be slept on -- all part of a trend toward criminalizing the homeless, a new study said on Wednesday.

While an old Christmas song encourages people to "put a penny in the old man's hat" at this time of year, the study found that in many of the largest U.S. cities, it is illegal for him to hold out his hat.

The Washington-based National Law Centre on Homelessness and Poverty said that 77 percent of 48 large American cities it surveyed had laws restricting begging, either banning it outright or prohibiting it in some public places.
Over half of these cities have engaged in police sweeps to clear homeless people from town, with some authorities jailing those repeatedly caught sleeping in public, the study said.

It said the "meanest streets" for the nation's homeless are in Atlanta, San Francisco, Dallas, New York and San Diego. The report said those cities have either passed broad restrictions against homeless people's conduct or made themselves inhospitable to the homeless population.
"In recent years, there has been a growing trend toward the 'criminalization' of homelessness in cities across the United States," the study said.
But it said many of the same cities that are rounding up or pushing out homeless people do not have enough shelters or places for someone down-on-his-luck to go.

"Over 700,000 people in the United States are homeless on any given night," the study said. But, "virtually none of the cities analysed in this report have a sufficient number of emergency shelter beds or transitional housing slots to accommodate their homeless residents."

The National Law Centre, established in 1989, advocates solutions to homelessness. For its study the centre interviewed homeless advocates, government representatives and organisations that provide services to homeless people.

"As opposed to attacking homeless people, cities should attack homelessness," the report concluded. It gave examples of some cities that were taking steps in this direction, including Miami's Dade County, which had implemented a 1 percent tax on meals at some restaurants to provide funding for facilities and services for homeless people.
Seattle has initiated a special housing levy to raise money for housing for homeless people, the report said.
